groups.label: Virtue and the Soul in State
groups.summary: Socrates establishes divine immutability and truthfulness as ethical standards while defining civic temperance, justice, and the tripartite division of the soul in terms of harmonious order and proper function.
groups.rationale: These early dialogue sections from Books II and IV construct the foundational concepts of virtue, divine nature, civic roles, and the inner structure of the human soul.

groups.label: Philosopher-Kings and Epistemology
groups.summary: Socrates introduces the rule of philosophers and rigorously distinguishes true knowledge of eternal forms from the fallible opinions of dreamers who focus on sensory particulars.
groups.rationale: All five items come from Book V, detailing the philosopher-king paradox and the epistemological separation between knowledge, opinion, and their respective objects.

groups.label: Reality, Pleasure, and Destiny
groups.summary: Across later books, Socrates divides intelligible and visible reality, exposes intermediate rest as an illusion of pleasure, and illustrates the soul's fateful choices and rebirth in the myth of Er.
groups.rationale: These dialogue passages from Books VI, IX, and X trace the ascent of understanding, the nature of true versus relative pleasure, and the ultimate destiny and choices of immortal souls.

groups.label: Editorial Syntheses of Themes
groups.summary: Editorial notes synthesize Plato's central metaphysical and ethical doctrines, covering dialectical method, divine nature, the Idea of the Good, civic and psychic justice, and Platonic psychology.
groups.rationale: These nodes belong to the editorial apparatus and paratext, providing retrospective philosophical summaries of dialectic, theology, metaphysics, justice, and the soul.
